subject: HTML artifact opening speed and resource cost after implementation
reader: Parker knows Terminal Delight and asked for fast artifact opening with 50 panes; he wants results, memory costs and limitations without reading Rust

sections.heading: Opening Speed
sections.text: You asked for the 2–3 second wait when opening HTML artifacts to disappear without keeping dozens of browser pages in memory. TD now prepares recent artifacts in advance; those prepared pages open in about a fifth of a second.

sections.heading: 01 The Wait Is Shorter
sections.text:
The preparation pays off when you press Alt+O. With 50 panes open, 100 prepared opens reached a fully painted viewport in 191 ms at the median and 264 ms at the 95th percentile . Every open used a valid prepared render. This meets the approved 250 ms median and 500 ms tail targets. 
 01 · Prepared Opening 
 The prepared path meets both latency targets under the 50-pane workload. Timings end at native paint submission. External Alt+O dispatch to the observation log measured 210 ms median and 311 ms p95; physical monitor presentation was not measured. 
Isolated Xvfb display: 49 hidden copies of one brief and 50 shell panes. This does not reproduce 50 running AI agents. Timing summary . 

Preparation makes the first opening eligible for the fast path. The previous cache already made repeats quick. On the formal brief, an uncached open still took 1.73 seconds median externally, against 2.00 seconds before. The 4× cold-opening target was not reached.

sections.heading: 02 Prepare Before the Click
sections.text:
TD watches the newest artifact in the focused pane. After a 400 ms pause, one worker prepares it at the size Alt+O will use. Up to nine recently visited panes remain candidates. Opening cancels preparation at the next browser-call boundary. 
 02 · Where the Work Goes 
 Nine recent panes select work; one worker does it. Each open validates the source, local assets, renderer settings and exact geometry. The first capture fits the viewport, and cache reads fetch visible images first. 
Drawn from preparation , cache and native rendering . 
A stable section anchor preserves your passage after edits; notes keep their identity. Changed or unknown assets trigger a fresh render. Once capture finishes, TD closes the browser page and can release the images when you leave the tab.

sections.heading: 03 What Stays in Memory
sections.text:
The cache lives under $XDG_CACHE_HOME/terminal-delight/pages , normally ~/.cache/terminal-delight/pages . Its 256 MiB budget is disk space. Open pages also need native images and the shared browser; their RAM cost varies with the document and allocator history. 
 03 · Visible Images Are Released 
 Closing released most of the added native graphics allocation in this sample. These are whole-window NVIDIA readings from a separate run. Hidden-view traces confirmed their browser pages closed; these counters do not measure all process memory. 
 Driver readings · Memory method and limits . 
In the 50-pane run, native processes used 333 MiB proportional RAM and Chromium used 156 MiB with the reader visible. Those totals include the terminal and shells. Allocator variation prevents a reliable per-document subtraction. Preparation skips work below 1 GiB available RAM and bounds source size, pixels and PNG output; these admission checks cannot guarantee a browser-RAM ceiling.

sections.heading: 04 Checked Through the Real Renderer
sections.text:
The same page retained identical height, all 10 note anchors and all 15 links. The first-viewport pixel difference averaged 0.0014 on a 0–255 scale. The native check confirmed note creation, automatic saving and survival across resize. Its harness then failed while polling a temporary reload state, so native reopening remains unverified by that run. Automated tests cover notes, cancellation, asset changes, hidden-buffer release and passage continuity. 
 Validation and reproduction link to raw timings, source and limitations. The implementation targets the next development wave for 0.5.3. Uncached complex pages remain the main performance limitation.
